### 2.3 The specification

- The element bound is `Number`, three times: "An array of two dimensions whose elements are a subtype of `Number` is a matrix", "A one-dimensional array whose elements are a subtype of `Number` is a vector" (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:152-170`); "all elements of vectors and matrices must be numbers" (`Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex:917`); the coercion chapter's example `trait Vector[\T extends Number\]` (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:230-236`).
- The arithmetic lives in algebra traits, not in `Number`. The chapter "Algebraic Constraints" gives `Ring[\T extends Ring[\T,⊕,⊖,⊗\], opr ⊕, opr ⊖, opr ⊗\]` and `Field` as self-typed traits with operators as static parameters and `where` clauses (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:1541-1545`, `:1761-1766`). The library that states that chapter exists only commented out, under `Library/incomplete/` (`reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md` section 1). The shipped library's `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` and `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` are its fixed-operator form.
- The revised numbers chapter says the flat tower: the number types "are siblings under the trait `Number`: each is a subtype of `Number`, and none is a subtype of another" (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:32-33`), and each carries the four traits at its own type (`:224-229`, `QQ`'s listing).
- A bound with two traits is the grammar's own: a static parameter is `Id Extends?` (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:40-41`), and `Extends` is `extends TraitType` or `extends { TraitType, ... }` as a trait's own clause is.
- A method asking more of `T` than its trait's bound is a `where` clause (`trait-parameters.tex:305-330`), "not yet supported" (`conversions-coercions.tex:15`), and no batch has planned it (`reviews/array-forks-now.md` section 3).
- So the specification says: elements are numbers; arithmetic is a self-typed algebra trait; a bound names what the body needs; asking per method waits for `where`. The two-trait bound makes no sentence of it false. A ring bound alone would make `overview.tex:917` false, since a ring that is not a number could then be an element (my reading).

### 2.4 The papers

- The self-type idiom is the papers' own: "The self-type idiom is realized with the **comprises** clause which contains the instantiation of the self type" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:580`); the Welterweight draft has a section "Self-typed generics" left commented out (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:195`). `T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` is that idiom applied to a bound.
- The per-method alternative is cited and never formalised: the dispatch paper's bibliography carries Day, Gruber, Liskov and Myers, "Subtypes vs. where clauses: constraining parametric polymorphism", OOPSLA 1995 (`Papers/Dispatch/main.bib:966-972`), the paper that where clauses come from. Nothing in `Papers/` gives Fortress's rule for them.
- The compiled encoding: "mentions of static parameters are replaced with their upper bounds" (`Papers/Implementation/MethodMapping.tex:134`). What a two-trait upper bound erases to is the code generator's question at the switch-over, not this fork's (section 2.2).
- The 2012 note on the return-type rule (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/2012-6-15 return type instantiation restrictions.txt`) concerns overloads with generic return types; the array family's overloads all fix `T` by their arguments, so it adds nothing here (my reading).

- **Generic arithmetic is bounded by the algebra trait at the element's type.** `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]` and `PROD[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3284-3301`, api `.fsi:1965-1976`), `SumReduction` and `ProdReduction` (`:3274`, `:3290`), `additiveIdentity` and `multiplicativeIdentity` (`:3223`, `:3240`), `SumProdReductionPair[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` (`:3257`). These are the revival's, written by route A's rung (`d846e3644`); the team's library has no two-trait static-parameter bound (`git show 75cca6683:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, grep for `extends {` in a static-parameter list, none), and neither is overloaded or has a closed trait among its bounds. The revival's tests pin the form under walk: `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericBesidePlainTwoBounds.fss` (a generic declaration with two open bounds beside plain ones, a valid overloading), and `XXXInferSeveralBoundsWalk.fss` (row 591). No compiled test has one.
- **The team's bound meant arithmetic.** Jan Maessen wrote `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` on 2007-12-13 (`1c492019f`) when `Number` was a ring at `Number` (section 2.7). The bodies' `e + v.get(i)` had the type `RR64` under that `Number`, not `T`, so even then the bodies were not well typed at `T`; the team never ran the checker on them (FACTS, "The shipped `RR64` ...").
- **Products are methods so that views override them.** `TransposedMatrix` overrides `scale`, `rmul` and `lmul` (`:2800-2802`), and the top-level `DOT` and juxtaposition forward to the methods (`:2463-2478`, `:2839-2871`). His diagonal does the same with `mul` (`explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fss:36-41`; POSITIONS, "The vocabulary's scalar drops and the diagonal"; row 299). A bound per method would need `where`; moving the products out of the traits would take the overrides with them.
- **A top-level operator carries its own bound.** `pmul[\T extends Number, nat k\]` (`:2460`), the sized `DOT`s, `SUM`, `PROD`: each generic function names what it needs. For the scalar block, whose eight operators are top-level, a bound per operator is the library's own form.

## 2. A valid element bound is not a proof of closure

The current vector bodies require `T + T -> T`, subtraction returning `T`, multiplication returning `T`, and a dot product returning `T`. The matrix multiplication body makes the requirement especially visible:

```fortress
pr : T = get(a,b) other.get(b,c)
res.put((a,c), res.get(a,c) + pr)
```

Yet their declaration says only `T extends Number`. Today's `Number` arithmetic returns `RR64`, and today's `SUM` returns `Number`. Neither signature establishes a result of every possible subtype `T`. After flattening, `Number` supplies no arithmetic at all. [A1, M3, R1]

**This is partly a pre-existing unchecked obligation, not a soundness defect newly created by route A.** The old count measured hierarchy/API checks and never reached the component bodies. Equipping `RR64` with `AdditiveGroup[\RR64\]` and `MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\]` supplies evidence for that particular scalar type; a body checked under only `T extends Number` cannot assume every leaf has those contracts. [A3, P2]

The earlier account that `Vector[T extends Number]` “stays valid” needs this qualification: numeric membership and the declaration's spelling survive; generic arithmetic-body validity has not been established. A copying operation such as C4's generic `gather` and an arithmetic operation such as `Matrix.mul` do not have the same requirements. [P3, M2]

A tempting blanket repair, requiring `MultiplicativeRing[T]` on every numeric container, is not justified by the chosen design either. The flat sketch gives `Integral[I]` `AdditiveGroup[I]`, not `MultiplicativeRing[I]`. Its multiplication returns `I`, but its exponentiation returns `RR64`, whereas the ring trait demands a result of `T`. C4 also needs integer vectors for keys and indices. Such a bound would exclude useful existing clients. [A1, A3, M2]

**Consequence for the library rung:** record the required capabilities per operation and check the actual generic bodies. Do not silently equate numeric membership, closed multiplication, ordering, and membership of the whole ring interface. Selecting a repair requires the project's normal design review; this note does not select a new trait or array architecture.

The inherited-code account also needs precision. `AdditiveGroup` declares `+` and supplies defaults for binary minus, unary minus and zero. `Vector` and `Matrix` implement all three addition/subtraction operators themselves and inherit zero; their views inherit those concrete container implementations. Complex `C`, by comparison, gets binary minus and juxtaposition from algebra defaults. These are distinct forms of reuse. None of those method signatures proves associativity or numerical stability. [A1, M3, A4]

- **Theorem 4.1 (p. 11:15).** "We first show that the more specific relation of method declarations is a partial order. It is clearly reflexive and transitive since the existential subtype relation is reflexive and transitive. (************************************************************
* \subsection*{Numeric hierarchy}
************************************************************)

(** Place holder for exclusions of AdditiveGroup **)
trait AnyAdditiveGroup end

(** Additive group making use of %+%.  Must define %+% and
    either unary or binary %-%. **)
trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T
    abstract opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self) : T
end

(** Place holder for exclusions of MultiplicativeRing **)
trait AnyMultiplicativeRing end

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
    Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    abstract getter one(): T
    abstract opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T
    (** Exponentiation need only deal with natural exponents. **)
    abstract opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T
end

trait Number extends { AnyAdditiveGroup, AnyMultiplicativeRing }
        comprises { RR64, RR32, QQ, AnyIntegral, IntLiteral }
    (** The value as a float, the explicit conversion into %RR64%. **)
    asFloat(self): RR64
    (** Two exact numbers of different types compare as rationals; a float
        compares with any number after %asFloat%, so an exact value equals
        its nearest float. **)
    opr =(self, other:Number):Boolean
end

(* Vector and Matrix operations and the scalar block run for an integer and a float element type, and matrix(v) puts the element type's own zero off the diagonal. *)

shown(v: Any): String = v.asString || " : " || v.ilkName

run(): () = do

component complex_ring
export Executable

(* C as a full citizen of the numeric tower: extends MultiplicativeRing.
   Defines only: one, +, unary -, TIMES, ^.
   Inherited: juxtaposition (= TIMES), binary - (= self + (-other)),
   zero (= self - self, a three-default chain). *)
object C(re: RR64, im: RR64) extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]
  getter one(): C = C(1.0, 0.0)
  opr +(self, other: C): C = C(re + other.re, im + other.im)
  opr -(self): C = C(-re, -im)
  opr TIMES(self, other: C): C =
    C((re other.re) - (im other.im), (im other.re) + (re other.im))
  opr ^(self, other: AnyIntegral): C =
    if other <= 0 then self.one else self (self^(other - 1)) end
end

show(tag: String, z: C): () = println(tag || z.re || " + " || z.im || "i")

run() = do
